mastery_goals.mastery_goal: Use evidence and models to distinguish observations, inferences, and testable physics explanations, and communicate what a representation or relationship means.
Explain Newton’s First Law and inertia to predict when an object’s motion remains unchanged or changes.
Represent and determine net force using vectors, then use the result to classify balanced and unbalanced situations.
Create, critique, and defend force models for real-world systems using evidence about interactions and motion.

learning_ladder.i_can: I can design, defend, or critique a force model for an unfamiliar real-world situation, using evidence to explain whether the object is in equilibrium or changing motion.
I can compare two competing explanations of the same force situation and justify which explanation better fits Newton’s First Law and the evidence.
I can connect a force diagram, written scenario, and motion description to explain how net force determines whether motion changes.
I can identify and correct a misconception about inertia, support force, net force, or equilibrium using a clear physics explanation.
I can determine net force in simple force situations and explain whether the forces are balanced or unbalanced.
I can draw and interpret simple force-vector diagrams using direction, arrow length, and labels.
I can define and recognize key terms such as force, inertia, net force, vector, support force, weight, and equilibrium.
I can recognize whether a situation involves rest, constant motion, or changing motion.

recurring_practices.framework_source_basis: Framework repeatedly calls for Concept Development, investigations/phenomenon tasks, whiteboarding, and synthesis/application work.
recurring_practices.what_student_evidence_looks_like: Student constructs, interprets, revises, or defends a model that connects the unit’s physical quantities and mechanisms.
recurring_practices.representations_contexts: force/vector diagrams, motion descriptions, $\Sigma F$ relationships, observations and evidence
recurring_practices.common_weaknesses: Models are treated as pictures only; labels/relationships are inconsistent; the model is not connected to a prediction or explanation.

mastery_goals.mastery_goal: Describe motion relative to a chosen reference frame and compare how the same motion can be described from different viewpoints.
Distinguish speed from velocity and use distance, time, and direction to describe motion quantitatively and conceptually.
Explain acceleration as change in velocity and analyze free-fall motion when gravity is the dominant force.
Build and critique multi-representation motion models using vectors, diagrams, tables, graphs, and equations.

learning_ladder.i_can: I can design, defend, or critique a motion model for an unfamiliar situation using words, data, graphs, formulas, and velocity vectors.
I can compare two competing motion explanations or models and justify which one better fits the evidence.
I can connect a motion graph, data table, velocity-vector diagram, and written scenario to explain how an object’s motion changes over time.
I can identify and correct a misconception about speed, velocity, acceleration, free fall, or reference frames using a clear physics explanation.
I can calculate speed, time, distance, acceleration, free-fall speed, or free-fall distance in simple situations and interpret the answer in context.
I can interpret motion diagrams, simple graphs, data tables, and velocity vectors to describe motion.
I can define and recognize key terms such as reference frame, speed, velocity, acceleration, free fall, and velocity vector.
I can recognize whether an object is at rest, moving at constant speed, changing speed, changing direction, or accelerating.

mastery_goals.mastery_goal: Apply Newton’s Second Law to relate net force, mass, and acceleration and explain how changing one quantity affects motion.
Model friction, weight, air resistance, and terminal-speed situations to explain free fall and nonfree fall.
Analyze Newton’s Third Law interactions by identifying equal-and-opposite forces acting on different objects.
Model projectile motion as simultaneous horizontal constant-velocity and vertical accelerated motion.

learning_ladder.i_can: I can design, defend, or critique a complete force-and-motion model for an unfamiliar real-world situation using force diagrams, Newton’s laws, motion evidence, and formulas.
I can compare competing explanations of a force, friction, falling, interaction, or projectile scenario and justify which explanation better fits the evidence.
I can connect force diagrams, motion descriptions, data tables, and formulas to explain how forces change motion.
I can identify and correct misconceptions about Newton’s Second Law, friction, mass and weight, air resistance, Newton’s Third Law, or projectile motion.
I can calculate force, mass, acceleration, weight, net force with friction, or basic projectile quantities in simple situations and interpret the result.
I can interpret force diagrams, interaction diagrams, free-fall diagrams, and projectile-motion models.
I can define and recognize key terms such as net force, acceleration, mass, weight, friction, air resistance, terminal speed, interaction, and projectile.
I can recognize whether a situation involves speeding up, slowing down, balanced force, unbalanced force, falling motion, or an interaction between objects.

mastery_goals.mastery_goal: Relate momentum, impulse, force, and time to explain and quantify changes in motion.
Use conservation of momentum to analyze collisions, explosions, and recoil after defining an appropriate system and considering external impulse.
Explain and calculate work, power, kinetic energy, and gravitational potential energy as connected descriptions of energy transfer and storage.
Use conservation of energy to explain transformations in mechanical and societal systems and evaluate real-world energy claims using evidence.

learning_ladder.i_can: I can design, defend, or critique a complete momentum-energy model for an unfamiliar real-world system using diagrams, data, equations, conservation laws, and evidence.
I can compare competing explanations of a collision, energy transfer, or energy-source claim and justify which explanation better fits physics evidence.
I can connect diagrams, before-and-after models, data tables, graphs, formulas, and written scenarios to explain momentum or energy changes.
I can identify and correct misconceptions about momentum, impulse, conservation, work, power, kinetic energy, potential energy, or energy efficiency.
I can calculate momentum, impulse, work, power, kinetic energy, potential energy, or simple before-and-after quantities and interpret the answer in context.
I can interpret collision diagrams, impulse situations, energy bar charts, work diagrams, and energy transformation models.
I can define and recognize key terms such as momentum, impulse, conservation, collision, work, power, kinetic energy, potential energy, and efficiency.
I can recognize whether a situation involves motion, collision, energy storage, energy transfer, energy transformation, or energy loss to the surroundings.

mastery_goals.mastery_goal: Describe wave motion using amplitude, wavelength, frequency, period, wave speed, and transverse/longitudinal representations.
Analyze wave interactions including superposition, interference, standing waves, and the Doppler effect.
Explain sound propagation, reflection, refraction, forced vibration, natural frequency, and resonance using a mechanical-wave model.
Use interference and frequency relationships to analyze beats and sound technologies or real-world phenomena.

learning_ladder.i_can: I can design, defend, or critique a complete wave or sound model for an unfamiliar situation using diagrams, data, equations, and evidence.
I can compare competing explanations of wave behavior, sound transmission, resonance, interference, or beats and justify which explanation better fits the evidence.
I can connect wave diagrams, sound models, data tables, graphs, formulas, and written scenarios to explain wave or sound behavior.
I can identify and correct misconceptions about wave speed, frequency, wavelength, sound transmission, Doppler effect, resonance, interference, or beats.
I can calculate wave speed, frequency, period, wavelength, echo distance, or beat frequency in simple situations and interpret the answer in context.
I can interpret transverse-wave diagrams, longitudinal-wave diagrams, interference diagrams, standing-wave diagrams, and sound-wave models.
I can define and recognize key terms such as vibration, wave, amplitude, wavelength, frequency, period, medium, compression, rarefaction, resonance, and interference.
I can recognize whether a situation involves vibration, wave motion, sound transmission, reflection, refraction, interference, resonance, or beats.

mastery_goals.mastery_goal: Explain light as electromagnetic radiation and connect wavelength, frequency, transmission, absorption, and shadow formation to observable behavior.
Use the law of reflection and ray models to explain reflected light, plane-mirror images, and diffuse reflection.
Explain and quantify refraction, dispersion, critical angle, and total internal reflection as consequences of changes in light speed across media.
Model image formation with lenses and apply optical principles to eyes, corrective lenses, fibers, and other systems.

learning_ladder.i_can: I can design, defend, or critique a complete optics model for an unfamiliar real-world situation using ray diagrams, evidence, formulas, and optical principles.
I can compare competing explanations of reflection, refraction, image formation, total internal reflection, or optical devices and justify which explanation better fits the evidence.
I can connect ray diagrams, wave models, lens diagrams, formulas, and written scenarios to explain how light behaves in optical systems.
I can identify and correct misconceptions about light travel, shadows, reflection, refraction, color, lenses, images, or total internal reflection.
I can calculate light speed relationships, index of refraction, reflection angles, refraction quantities, lens quantities, or magnification in simple situations and interpret the answer in context.
I can interpret light-ray diagrams, mirror diagrams, refraction diagrams, total internal reflection diagrams, and lens diagrams.
I can define and recognize key terms such as electromagnetic wave, transparent, opaque, reflection, normal, refraction, lens, focal point, real image, virtual image, and total internal reflection.
I can recognize whether a situation involves light travel, absorption, transmission, reflection, refraction, dispersion, image formation, or optical technology.

mastery_goals.mastery_goal: Explain charge interactions, conservation of charge, conductors/insulators, and charging processes with particle and interaction models.
Explain voltage as energy per charge and current as charge flow in a complete circuit.
Relate voltage, current, resistance, power, and electrical energy quantitatively and interpret data or graphs describing components/devices.
Analyze series, parallel, and mixed circuits by tracing paths and explaining how changes affect current, voltage, equivalent resistance, brightness, and safety.

learning_ladder.i_can: I can design, defend, or critique a complete electric-circuit model for an unfamiliar real-world system using diagrams, evidence, formulas, and circuit principles.
I can compare competing explanations of charge behavior, voltage, current, resistance, power, or circuit design and justify which explanation better fits the evidence.
I can connect circuit diagrams, data tables, formulas, energy-transfer models, and written scenarios to explain electrical behavior.
I can identify and correct misconceptions about charge, static electricity, voltage, current, resistance, Ohm’s Law, power, or series and parallel circuits.
I can calculate electric force, voltage, current, resistance, power, energy use, or equivalent resistance in simple situations and interpret the answer in context.
I can interpret charge diagrams, electric-force diagrams, circuit diagrams, voltage-current graphs, and series/parallel models.
I can define and recognize key terms such as charge, conductor, insulator, voltage, current, resistance, circuit, power, energy, series, and parallel.
I can recognize whether a situation involves static charge, charge transfer, current, voltage, resistance, electrical energy transfer, or a complete circuit.

recurring_practices.what_student_evidence_looks_like: Student makes a physics claim, cites appropriate evidence or representation, and connects that evidence to the governing model or relationship.
recurring_practices.representations_contexts: charge distributions, force/interaction models, circuit schematics, I-V data/graphs, electrical relationships
recurring_practices.common_weaknesses: Claim without evidence; evidence listed without reasoning; vocabulary used without explaining the causal/physical connection.

mastery_goals.mastery_goal: Explain magnetic poles, fields, and domains using field representations and evidence from magnetic interactions.
Explain how electric current produces magnetic fields and how coils/cores create controllable electromagnets.
Analyze magnetic forces on moving charges and current-carrying wires using direction, field, motion/current, and source-supported quantitative relationships.
Explain electromagnetic induction, generators, alternating current, transformers, and modern systems as linked field/current processes and energy transformations.

learning_ladder.i_can: I can design, defend, or critique a complete electromagnetic-system model for an unfamiliar real-world technology using fields, forces, current, induction, energy transformations, formulas, and evidence.
I can compare competing explanations of magnetic fields, electromagnets, magnetic forces, generators, transformers, or electromagnetic devices and justify which explanation better fits the evidence.
I can connect field diagrams, current diagrams, force diagrams, induction models, formulas, and written scenarios to explain electromagnetic behavior.
I can identify and correct misconceptions about magnets, magnetic fields, domains, electromagnets, magnetic forces, induction, generators, or energy in electromagnetic systems.
I can calculate magnetic force, magnetic field strength, transformer voltage, or electric power in simple situations and interpret the answer in context.
I can interpret magnetic field diagrams, domain diagrams, electromagnet diagrams, magnetic-force diagrams, generator diagrams, and AC graphs.
I can define and recognize key terms such as magnetic pole, magnetic field, domain, electromagnet, magnetic force, induction, generator, alternating current, and transformer.
I can recognize whether a situation involves magnetic attraction or repulsion, a magnetic field, current-produced magnetism, magnetic force, induction, or electromagnetic technology.

recurring_practices.framework_source_basis: Framework repeatedly calls for Concept Development, investigations/phenomenon tasks, whiteboarding, and synthesis/application work.
recurring_practices.what_student_evidence_looks_like: Student constructs, interprets, revises, or defends a model that connects the unit’s physical quantities and mechanisms.
recurring_practices.representations_contexts: magnetic field/domain diagrams, current/coil models, force diagrams, generator/transformer models, AC graphs and energy flows
recurring_practices.common_weaknesses: Models are treated as pictures only; labels/relationships are inconsistent; the model is not connected to a prediction or explanation.

recurring_practices.framework_source_basis: Framework embeds investigations, Formula Examples, ranking/error-analysis tasks, and whiteboarding across the unit.
recurring_practices.what_student_evidence_looks_like: Student extracts a physical relationship from a graph, table, diagram, observation set, or other representation and translates it into words or another representation.
recurring_practices.representations_contexts: magnetic field/domain diagrams, current/coil models, force diagrams, generator/transformer models, AC graphs and energy flows
recurring_practices.common_weaknesses: Reading a graph/diagram superficially; confusing what axes/arrows/regions represent; switching representations without preserving the physical relationship.

recurring_practices.framework_source_basis: Framework includes Formula Examples and practice while explicitly emphasizing conceptual understanding before computation.
recurring_practices.what_student_evidence_looks_like: Student selects and interprets source-supported relationships involving magnetic-force/field, transformer, and electric-power relationships, uses units/variables coherently, and explains what a result means.
recurring_practices.representations_contexts: magnetic field/domain diagrams, current/coil models, force diagrams, generator/transformer models, AC graphs and energy flows
recurring_practices.common_weaknesses: Equation hunting without a model; arithmetic with no interpretation; incorrect units or variable meaning; computation overriding conceptual constraints.

recurring_practices.framework_source_basis: Every section includes an Investigation / Lab / Phenomenon Task in the framework, with discussion and whiteboarding.
recurring_practices.what_student_evidence_looks_like: Student identifies what evidence would test a claim or model, uses observations/data appropriately, and evaluates whether results support the explanation.
recurring_practices.representations_contexts: magnetic field/domain diagrams, current/coil models, force diagrams, generator/transformer models, AC graphs and energy flows
recurring_practices.common_weaknesses: Treating one observation as proof; failing to control/identify relevant variables; reporting data without connecting it to the claim or model.
